messages.author: 43e2e19dd6bd2992
messages.subject: Problems with plotNuse
parts:
Hi Ju,

I was posting the speed question because Paul was wanting things to
get sped up, so I would like to have well informed people be able to
respond to that as well. So I started a new question for the plot part
of your question.

But in terms of the plot... this is probably a stupid response, but I
never use dev.print. I am assuming since you use dev.print, you got
the picture on your screen and want to save it. Is the behavior any
different if you don't try to post-save, but send directly to a
separate printing device? For example,

pdf("NUSEPlots.pdf")
plotNuse(qam)
dev.off()

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.author: 185f4d4fdb048fb8
messages.subject: Re: [aroma.affymetrix] Problems with plotNuse
parts:
On 11/8/07, epurdom <epu...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Ju,
>
> I was posting the speed question because Paul was wanting things to
> get sped up, so I would like to have well informed people be able to
> respond to that as well. So I started a new question for the plot part
> of your question.
>
> But in terms of the plot... this is probably a stupid response, but I
> never use dev.print. I am assuming since you use dev.print, you got
> the picture on your screen and want to save it. Is the behavior any
> different if you don't try to post-save, but send directly to a
> separate printing device? For example,
>
> pdf("NUSEPlots.pdf")
> plotNuse(qam)
> dev.off()

Yes, setting up the output device before calling a plot function in R
is better. It will generate better looking graphs because R optimizes
the layout to the target device. When using dev.print(), R cannot do
this.

However, the time to generate the plot will be roughly the same.

The QualityAssementModel class, which plotNuse() operates on, was
written some time ago by Ken Simpson. It has partly been optimized
for speed, but not in full, so maybe some improvements can be done to
the implementation.

However, if you look at the plotNuse.QualityAssementModel function
(please do that), you'll see that there several intermediate steps
done and some of these takes time. Some of the methods
(automagically) cache their results to file so that when calling them
the next time will be much faster.

Again, use the 'verbose' argument to track down what takes time - it
often makes sense we you see it.

Moreover, to calculate an approximate NUSE, you can specify the
fraction of data, in (0,1], to be used by using argument 'subset'.
That way not all data has to be loaded and you will still get
reasonable results.

Example:

verbose <- Verbose(threshold=-30);
timestampOn(verbose);
...
plotNuse(qam, subset=1/3, verbose=verbose);

to track down what takes time.

/Henrik

>
> Best,
> Elizabeth
>
>
> >
>

Hi,

Yes, using pdf and dev.off it creates the pdf with RLE, NUSE pltos.
But with >120 samples,
the fig. is tough to read, i.e. to find which samples are giving the
high values. Is there any way
to break it up in say 10 samples? i.e. for 120 samples, have 12
figures? Then with par()
I can put all in a page or two.

Thanks!
Amrita.
